Example: A person running towards the sunset
Underspecification: Direction of movement, speed, gait phase
Proper Representation: 2D canvas with drawable motion path + directional stroke
Literature Notes: TaleBrush demonstrated that sketch trajectories effectively control spatial and narrative outcomes. The shape of a drawn line directly maps to the path a subject takes. For "flying in circles," a drawn circular stroke resolves ambiguity about arc shape, radius, and flight pattern. The sketching metaphor naturally extends to 3D movement when combined with altitude annotation (e.g., stroke thickness or a separate layer).

Example: A person waving goodbye
Underspecification: Hand position, finger spread, wave phase
Proper Representation: Gesture gallery with hand pose variants
Literature Notes: Block and Detail showed that blocking strokes effectively communicate form intent without requiring detailed drawing skill—the system interprets rough strokes as structural scaffolding. For abstract emotional descriptors like "confident," which map to many possible body poses, users can draw minimal blocking strokes indicating key postural elements: an upright spine line (vs. curved for "timid"), wide shoulder line (vs. narrow for "insecure"), raised chin angle (vs. lowered for "sad"). This decomposes the abstract emotion into concrete spatial posture cues that the system can interpret, resolving the ambiguity without requiring users to articulate pose details in text or draw anatomically correct figures.

Example: A woman with a mysterious smile
Underspecification: Lip curvature, eye narrowing, eyebrow position
Proper Representation: Semantic expression sliders with feedforward previews; multiple sliders controlling facial attribute dimensions (smile intensity, eye narrowing, brow position)
Literature Notes: GANSlider established that multiple sliders with feedforward previews effectively control generative model outputs, and that previews significantly improve user accuracy despite adding some cognitive load. For ambiguous expressions like "mysterious smile," the ambiguity lies in the specific combination of facial attributes, how much smile curvature, how narrowed the eyes, how raised the eyebrows. Slider-based control decomposes the abstract term "mysterious" into manipulable facial dimensions, letting users define their interpretation through continuous adjustment rather than text iteration. The feedforward preview is critical: users can see how each slider affects the expression before committing, enabling precise specification of nuanced expressions that fall between discrete categories.

Example: A woman in a red dress
Underspecification: Exact hue (crimson vs scarlet vs burgundy), saturation, brightness
Proper Representation: Color picker with sample-and-tweak workflow, palette presets for named color variants (crimson, scarlet, burgundy) + precision picker for fine-tuning sampled colors
Literature Notes: Color Portraits (CHI 2015) found that designers rarely work with colors in isolation: 7 of 8 participants sampled colors from external references (photographs, websites, physical objects) and then tweaked them before applying, identifying "sampling and tweaking individual colors" as a fundamental color manipulation activity. Palette, Purpose, Prototype (CHI 2024) found that designers translate abstract intentions into specific colors through reference materials, with one team extracting that "for 'freshness' we had the lime" from collected visuals. For an ambiguous color term like "red," which could mean crimson, scarlet, burgundy, or dozens of other hues, this sample-and-tweak workflow directly resolves the ambiguity: users can sample their intended red from a reference image or select from named presets representing common interpretations, then fine-tune to their exact specification rather than iterating through text descriptions.

Example: A bird in the corner of the image
Underspecification: Which corner, exact distance from edges, size relative to frame
Proper Representation: Spatial canvas with region painting and draggable placeholders. Users paint or draw regions to specify where objects should appear
Representation Source: WorldSmith (Dang et al., UIST 2023); GenTune (Wang et al., UIST 2025); LayoutDiffusion (Zheng et al., 2023)
Literature Notes: LayoutDiffusion established that "problems such as missing objects and incorrectly generating objects' positions...occur in state-of-the-art text-guided diffusion models...mainly due to the ambiguity of the text and its weakness in precisely expressing the position of the image space." WorldSmith (UIST 2023) found that "participants tend to create their world models in parts, using sketching and text inputs to communicate positional information," and introduced region descriptions that "permit users to spatially specify where content should generate on the canvas" by linking painted regions to prompt segments via color coding. GenTune (UIST 2025) extended this by enabling designers to "select any element in a generated image, trace it back to the corresponding prompt labels"—demonstrating that spatial-to-prompt traceability improves control. For ambiguous absolute positions like "in the corner," which doesn't specify which corner or exact distance from edges, a spatial canvas with region painting directly resolves the ambiguity through visual placement rather than textual description.

Example: A large tree in a meadow
Underspecification: Height in pixels, proportion of frame, trunk width
Proper Representation: Resizable bounding box with proportional scale reference — draggable box handles for size control
Representation Source: GLIGEN (Li et al., CVPR 2023); Proportion ControlNet (2025); LayoutDiffusion (Zheng et al., 2023); WorldSmith (Dang et al., UIST 2023)
Literature Notes: GLIGEN demonstrated that bounding boxes effectively encode both "position and size" as unified spatial information, with their GUI enabling users to "specify the location and size of multiple objects in the image." The Proportion ControlNet (2025) extended this specifically for artistic control, using "bounding boxes to dictate the position and scale of objects"—noting that bounding boxes provide "a higher level of abstraction, defining the semantic space an object should occupy" while allowing artists to "easily apply proportion rules like the rule of thirds." WorldSmith (UIST 2023) found that users naturally communicate size through spatial means rather than text, with "participants tend[ing] to create their world models in parts, using sketching and text inputs to communicate positional information." For ambiguous size terms like "large", which doesn't specify proportion of frame, absolute dimensions, or relative scale, a resizable bounding box directly encodes the intended size as a visual proportion, resolving the ambiguity through direct manipulation rather than text iteration.

Example: A forest with trees in the foreground
Underspecification: Depth position, overlap handling, atmospheric perspective
Proper Representation: Layer panel with depth ordering + grayscale depth map painter, visual layer stack (like Photoshop layers) showing foreground-to-background ordering
Representation Source: Evaluating Spatial Relations in T2I Models (2024); OOSIS (2025); LayeringDiff (Kang et al., 2025); Lasagna (Yang et al., 2025); WorldSmith (Dang et al., UIST 2023); ControlNet Depth (Zhang & Agrawala, 2023)
Literature Notes: Depth terms like "in the background" and "in front of" are among the most ambiguous spatial relations for text-to-image models. Evaluating Spatial Relations in T2I Models (2024) found that "In Front Of and Behind achieved 35.8% and 27.5% accuracy respectively for T2I models." OOSIS (2025) further established that "a sofa can be to the left of a person... but it could be either behind or in front of the person in the corresponding 3D scene. Standard instance segmentation cannot determine this depth relationship." Professional creative tools address this through layered representations, as LayeringDiff notes, "Layers have become indispensable tools for professional artists, allowing them to build a hierarchical structure that enables independent control over individual visual elements." For technical implementation, ControlNet Depth uses grayscale depth maps where "brighter areas (closer to white) indicate objects that are closer, while darker areas (closer to black) indicate objects that are farther away," enabling the model to "correctly interpret spatial relationships."
